analysis.one_liner: Lets states redirect federal health dollars into their own universal health care systems.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever getting a vote; three Democratic senators backed it and no one else signed on before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a new waiver to the Affordable Care Act letting any state apply to combine its federal health funding — Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, insurance subsidies, and more — into one state-run health plan covering all residents. States would have to cover at least 95% of residents within five years, offer benefits at least as generous as what federal programs provide, and keep the arrangement budget-neutral for the federal government. It was introduced in July 2024 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and Congress ended without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of states that choose to participate: everyone in the state would get health coverage through one publicly administered plan, including people currently uninsured or paying high premiums and deductibles. People would keep one coverage card regardless of job changes, and states must cover reproductive health care including abortion, contraception, and gender-affirming care. States gain flexibility to design their own system and to reinvest any administrative savings into care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: State residents who lack affordable coverage

how_it_helps.text: A state could waive ACA market rules, Medicaid rules, Medicare, CHIP, federal employee coverage, and ACA subsidies and fold that funding into one state universal health plan covering all residents [S2].
States must pass a plan covering at least 95% of residents within five years, with coverage and cost-sharing at least as affordable as the federal programs it replaces [S2].
The state plan must be publicly administered and must cover reproductive health care services, including abortion, contraception, and gender-affirming care [S2].

Federal money that would otherwise be spent in the state on those programs, including premium tax credits and caseload growth adjusted for health inflation, would be paid to the state instead, and any savings could be reinvested in health services [S2].
Two or more neighboring states could submit a single joint application to run one regional plan together [S2].

analysis.who_pays: State taxpayers in participating states. The federal contribution is capped at what the federal government was already spending in the state, budget-neutral, so a state choosing this path would have to raise revenue to cover everyone — the bill does not itself pay for universal coverage. Insurers that sell individual and employer coverage in adopting states would lose most of that business.

drawbacks.text: The federal passthrough is explicitly budget-neutral, so a participating state must make up the full difference between current federal funding and the cost of covering everyone — a major new state tax burden [S2].

People who like their current employer or private coverage would lose it in an adopting state, where duplicative essential coverage would be restricted — a real change for millions who did not ask for it [S2].
A state that misses the 95% coverage target after a review and a 12-month grace period can have its waiver terminated by the Secretary, creating uncertainty for a system built to last [S2].

The waiver sweeps in Medicare, TRICARE, and federal employee coverage — programs whose funding rules and beneficiary expectations were not designed to be pooled into a state plan, raising hard transition questions [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a state willing to raise the revenue, the bill offers a genuine path to covering everyone at lower administrative cost, with strong protections on generosity, affordability, and reproductive care built into the terms. The main cost is honest: someone has to pay for universal coverage, and the bill deliberately leaves that to each state's taxpayers. The tradeoff is serious but transparent — it is a permit, not a free ride.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Finance Committee from the day it was introduced until Congress ended in January 2025, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Markey introduced the bill on July 25, 2024, with Sens. Warren and Merkley, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S1].
Only two senators cosponsored the bill, both Democrats [S3].
The action history shows no further activity after the referral — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — and the 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and other parties with a stake in the existing coverage system are better off, since no state can pursue a single-payer pathway and nothing about the current employer-based and private insurance markets changed. The three sponsoring senators gained nothing; the bill's state-level universal coverage route is closed for now.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and defenders of the status quo

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Finance Committee in July 2024 [S1].

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.role: Committee where the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the remainder of the 118th Congress [S4].

against.name: Private health insurers
against.role: Industry affected by state single-payer plans
against.what_they_did: Had no need to lobby this bill directly; three sponsors and no committee action meant it posed no real threat.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a vote where a partisan split could be recorded [S3].

industries.note: In any state that adopts the waiver, the state plan replaces most private coverage for essential benefits, and the state must run public education about restrictions on duplicative private insurance — their core market would shrink sharply. Insurers could still sell coverage for benefits outside the state plan [S2].

Universal coverage would mean far fewer uninsured patients and less uncompensated care, but a publicly administered state plan would likely pay less per service than private insurers do. Providers in adopting states would trade volume for lower rates.

A single publicly administered state plan covering everyone is a much stronger negotiating position than today's fragmented private market, putting downward pressure on drug prices in adopting states.

Employers in an adopting state could stop administering complex health benefits, a real administrative lift off their books, though they would face part of the state's new financing burden through taxes.
